title: Deriving Scaling Laws for OpenEuroLLM Models: Learning Rate, Batch Size and Loss
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 28 Aug 2026]
    Title:Deriving Scaling Laws for OpenEuroLLM Models: Learning Rate, Batch Size and Loss
View PDF
            Abstract:We study the scaling behavior of learning rate and batch size in pretraining dense large language models on English-prevalent corpora. Beyond scaling \textit{jointly optimal} learning rates and batch sizes, we investigate their \textit{marginal} evolution with model capacity and data scale and develop a model that captures these relationships. As we employ a Warmup-Stable-Decay learning rate schedule, we further investigate the gains from learning rate annealing over a broad range of hyperparameters settings, models and data budgets, and whether the optimal learning rate and batch size \textit{transfer} between the stable and decay phases. Finally, we characterize the dependence of loss on model capacity and dataset size, evaluating recently proposed scaling forms that explicitly model their interaction. We find these approaches particularly effective at capturing both undertraining and overtraining regimes across our experiments. This study establishes a first baseline and scaling procedure for the development of future OpenEuroLLM models. We open-source the complete collection of pretraining runs used in this study.

report.summary: New OpenEuroLLM paper derives scaling laws for learning rate, batch size, and loss to guide efficient pretraining of large language models.
report.background: Training large language models efficiently requires choosing hyperparameters like learning rate and batch size that scale predictably with model size and data volume. Most existing scaling laws focus on loss as a function of compute, but practical training also needs guidance on how learning rate and batch size should evolve as models grow. This study, part of the OpenEuroLLM initiative, systematically runs hundreds of pretraining experiments on English-prevalent corpora. It examines both jointly optimal settings and marginal changes of hyperparameters with model capacity and data scale. Using a Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule, the authors also test whether optimal settings transfer from stable training to the decay phase, and whether newer loss scaling forms that model model-data interaction can capture undertrained and overtrained regimes. The paper open-sources all pretraining runs, establishing a first reproducible baseline for future OpenEuroLLM models.
key_points: The paper provides a baseline for scaling learning rate and batch size across model sizes and data budgets. Rather than treating these hyperparameters as fixed, the authors derive formulas showing how they should marginally change as capacity and data grow, enabling more efficient tuning than grid search.

A key contribution is analyzing a Warmup-Stable-Decay learning rate schedule. The study finds that gains from annealing are consistent across many settings, and that optimal learning rate and batch size do not always transfer perfectly between stable and decay phases, which has practical implications for training recipes.

The work evaluates recent scaling forms that explicitly model the interaction between model capacity and dataset size. These forms outperform simpler power laws when models are undertrained or overtrained, providing a more accurate predictor of final loss across diverse experimental configurations.

All pretraining runs are open-sourced. This transparency lets other researchers replicate the scaling analyses, test new hypotheses, and build on the data without repeating expensive training runs, which is especially valuable for the open-source AI community.

The study is tied to the OpenEuroLLM project, aiming to develop open European LLMs. By deriving scaling laws on English-prevalent data first, it lays groundwork for future multilingual extensions and more compute-efficient model development in that initiative.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this research reduces the guesswork in large-scale training: developers can predict near-optimal learning rate and batch size before spending millions on compute, directly cutting costs and improving training stability. For researchers and open-source projects like OpenEuroLLM, the released training runs offer a shared empirical foundation to test scaling theories, accelerating iterative improvements. For regular users, more efficient pretraining may lead to better-performing open models trained on smaller budgets, potentially increasing competition with proprietary systems. The finding that interaction-based scaling forms handle both under- and overtraining is particularly useful for organizations working with limited data, helping them decide whether to add data or parameters.
report.tools: Watch the OpenEuroLLM repository and their Hugging Face organization for released model checkpoints and training configs. For scaling-law analysis, the community often uses the Chinchilla-inspired equations implemented in libraries like `llm-scaling` or frameworks such as EleutherAI's `lm-evaluation-harness` to validate loss predictions. Also follow the paper's open-sourced training runs on GitHub or DagsHub, which can serve as a dataset for derivative studies on hyperparameter scaling.
